IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON POWER SYSTEMS, VOL. 35, NO. 2, MARCH 2020 831
Kriging Assisted Surrogate Evolutionary
Computation to Solve Optimal Power
Flow Problems
Zhida Deng , Mihai D. Rotaru , Member , IEEE, and Jan K. Sykulski , Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—This paper proposes a Kriging assisted strategy to
expedite evolutionary computation for solving Optimal Power Flow
(OPF) problems. First, two algorithms were developed–a Kriging
Assisted Genetic Algorithm (KAGA) and a Kriging Assisted Parti-
cle Swarm Optimization (KAPSO) - and tested using unconstrained
benchmark functions; it was found that both algorithms provided
reliable and robust solutions. Accordingly, KAGA and KAPSO
were selected and tested on the IEEE 30 and 118 bus systems for
minimizing generation costs and active power losses. It is shown
that the proposed KAPSO outperforms other algorithms, especially
in terms of the computation time. In reference to the solution quality
yielded by KAGA and KAPSO, the proposed Kriging assisted
strategy offers a promising method to improve the performance
of evolutionary based computation when solving OPF problems.
Index Terms—Optimal power ﬂow, genetic algorithm, particle
swarm optimization, Kriging, surrogate modelling, evolutionary
computation.
I. I NTRODUCTION
S
INCE the concept of Optimal Power Flow (OPF) was ﬁrst
introduced as a Non-Linear Programming (NLP) problem
by Carpentier [1] for solving Economic Dispatch (ED) problems,
it has been used as an essential tool in planning, operating, and
dealing with energy management aspects of power systems. The
complexity of the problem depends critically on the selection of
objective functions and design variables due to the combinatorial
nature of the components and their connections. Mathematically,
the formulation leads to a large-scale, non-convex, non-linear,
highly constrained optimization problem where the continuous
(e.g., generator voltage magnitudes, generator active power
outputs) and discrete (e.g., transformer taps, switch shunts)
variables are optimized within speciﬁed constraints to optimize
the desired objectives, such as generation cost, active power loss,
improved transient stability, etc.
Over the years Linear Programming (LP) [2], Quadratic Pro-
gramming (QP) [3], Mix-Integer Linear Programming (MILP)
[4] and Mix-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MINLP) [5]

have been proposed to efﬁciently deﬁne the OPF problems,
while the selection of the programming formulation usually
implicates the solution method [6]. For example, LP requires
linearizing the objective function and constraints, whereas QP
is a variant of NLP in which the objective function is expressed
as a quadratic form and the constraints are linearized. The deter-
ministic methods–like the Simplex Method [7] and Sequential
Linear Programming Method [2], Sequential Quadratic Pro-
gramming Method [8], Newton Based Method [9] and Interior
Point Method (IPM) [10], have been applied for many years
to solve the practical OPF problems in the form of LP , QP
and NLP , respectively. Because the constraints are efﬁciently
handled (e.g., IPM converts a constrained OPF problem into
an unconstrained one by introducing a Lagrangian objective
function) and they produce reasonable optimal solutions (e.g.,
Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions) at excellent computational
speed. These methods, however, rely strongly on the convexity
of the problem (while OPF problems are naturally non-convex)
and the choice of an initial starting point in the search for an
optimal solution, thus do not guarantee to converge to a global
optimum. Moreover, although suitable MILP and especially
MINLP forms have been proposed to accurately capture the
behavior of the OPF problems, deterministic methods may not
be appropriate forthe solution of complex optimization tasks.
This is due to the fact that deterministic methods generally
consider the OPF problems as being continuous, cannot easily
handle discrete variables, and the derivative of the objective
function may not always be available. To use a deterministic
method, a compromise may have to be made in terms of relia-
bility, accuracy and computation efﬁciency [11]. Recent years,
evolutionary based algorithms (i.e., non-deterministic methods)
have attracted attention in academic research, because they can
easily deal with the drawbacks of the deterministic methods.
Theoretically, the global optimum can always be found after
many iterations by using the non-deterministic methods–such
as Genetic Algorithm (GA) [12], Particle Swarm Optimization
(PSO) [13] and Simulated Annealing (SA) [14]. However, the
computational cost dramatically increases due to a large number
of calls for objective function evaluation (e.g., full AC power
ﬂow analysis) and this limits the application of evolutionary
computation in real-time OPF situations.
All reported OPF methodologies, including deterministic and
non-deterministic, have advantages in some aspects and weak-
nesses in others [11]. Surrogate modelling techniques were

introduced some time ago in optimization community but have
not been applied to solve OPF problems. The focus on sur-
rogate assisted evolutionary optimization for accelerating the
overall computational speed by reducing the total number of
calls to objective function evaluation started in 2002 during the
Genetic and Evolutionary Computation Conference (GECCO)
[15]. To summarize, the strategies for combining surrogates with
evolutionary computation were classiﬁed into three categories:
individual-based, population-based and generation-based [16].
Thus the ﬁtness of some individuals, populations or generations
is evaluated using a real objective function, while others are esti-
mated by a surrogate model. By properly managing a surrogate
model the number of function evaluations can be reduced and
thus the CPU time improved. A variety of surrogate modelling
methods exist, including Polynomial Regression, Radial Basis
Function, Neural Networks and Kriging (also known as Gaus-
sian Processes). Kriging proved to be the most successful surro-
gate method in electromagnetic design as argued and reported
by the Southampton group [16], [17]. However, the application
of Kriging has so far been limited to relatively small-scale
optimization tasks, whereas OPF problems tend to have a large
number of variables. The issue arises due to the need to invert
a large correlation matrix with associated O( n3) computational
cost and O(n3) storage requirements [19], wheren is the sample
size. Furthermore, the low ﬁdelity of a surrogate model may
cause the evolutionary optimization to fall into a local optimum
trap.
This paper exploits the Kriging method to reduce the compu-
tational burden associated with evolutionary solutions of OPF
problems. An individual-focused strategy–which efﬁciently ad-
dresses the ﬁdelity, computational cost and storage requirements
of using Kriging in combination with evolutionary computation–
is proposed. A Euclidean distance based method is developed
to balance exploitation and exploration when selecting a par-
ticle (individual) for updating the population and the Krig-
ing sample set. To illustrate the strategy, a Kriging Assisted
Genetic Algorithm (KAGA) and a Kriging Assisted Particle
Swarm Optimization (KAPSO) are developed and tested on
four benchmark functions with results compared with the GA
and the PSO. KAGA and KAPSO are then chosen due to their
reliable and robust performance and applied to the IEEE 30
and 118 bus systems for minimizing the generation cost and
active power losses. The ensuing solutions are compared with
published results.

III. K RIGING ASSISTED EVOLUTIONARY COMPUTA TION
Amongst various non-deterministic methods, GA and PSO
are best known with proven computational efﬁciency. The meth-
ods will be mentioned only brieﬂy as a more detailed description
may be found for example in [21]. A combination of Kriging
with GA and PSO is the proposed novel approach here, but it
should be emphasized that this new strategy may also be applied
to other evolutionary algorithms.
A. Kriging

uses observed data (samples) to create a response surface to
estimate the values of the objective function at unobserved

B. Proposed Individual-Based Strategy
1) Initialization: This deﬁnes the population size, the maxi-
mum number of iterations and the essential parameters for GA
or PSO. Then a real-valued population is randomly generated
consisting of a speciﬁed number of individuals whose ﬁtness is
evaluated; this is later used to build a Kriging model.
2) Updating the Individuals: For GA, the arithmetic
crossover [24] and Gaussian mutation [24], [25] operators are
employed to update the individuals; for PSO, the type 1′′ con-
striction coefﬁcients [27] are used to calculate the velocity of
each particle for updating the swarm.
3) Evaluate the Fitness: The Kriging model is constructed
using the given samples (i.e., initial population), for estimating
the ﬁtness and MSE of all updated individuals. A Bayesian based
technique called Expected Improvement (EI) [28] is applied to
guide the selection of which individuals should be evaluated
using the real objective function. The calculation of EI is based
on the estimated MSE of individuals as

4) Updating the Population and Samples: A possible strat-
egy, as recommended in [16], is to have a certain number of
individuals, based on the estimated ﬁtness, that are selected and
re-evaluated using the real objective function for updating the
population. However, this may push the optimization process
towards a local optimum and result in unwanted additional FEs,
should the constructed surrogate model have low ﬁdelity or be
over-ﬁtted. We propose that the inﬁlling point should replace the
individual (for KAGA) or personal best (for KAPSO) with the
worst ﬁtness. Even if the ﬁtness of an inﬁlling point is not better
than the current worst ﬁtness of an individual or the personal
best, a point selected by the maximum EI should be used as a
replacement because of the information it contains.
In general, the inﬁlling points need to be iteratively added
into the samples to build a global Kriging model; however, this
might signiﬁcantly increase the computational cost and require
large amounts of physical memory, due to the need to invert a big
correlation matrix as seen from (25) and (26). In our proposed
strategy, the inﬁlling point will replace the best sample point
only if the inﬁlling ﬁtness is better than or equal to the best
sample; otherwise, the inﬁlling point will replace the sample
with a worst ﬁtness. This is claimed to be an effective way to
alleviate the computing issues of using Kriging, and a local
surrogate model around the optimal solution region could be
eventually constructed.

mum, a mutation strategy adopted from [29] is used to ‘jump
out’ of the local optimum

In this Elitist Learning Strategy (ELS), only one dimension
is mutated at a time because the local optimum may actually
belong to the global best. After evaluating the mutated local best
position, the population–or the individuals, the personal best and

Moreover, in a similar way as when updating the population, the
mutated individual (or particle) will be used even if it possesses
a poor ﬁtness than the current worst ﬁtness in the population,
because of its usefulness in global searching.
The proposed algorithm then goes back to step 2 and continues
until the predeﬁned maximum iteration number is reached or
another termination criterion is met (e.g., the standard deviation
of a sample smaller than a deﬁned value).
C. Tests Using Benchmark Optimization Functions
Before applying to real OPF problems the two algorithms
were tested using four multimodal benchmark functions (Ack-
ley, Levy, Rastrigin and Schwefel functions, details of which
may be found in [30]). All test functions used 50 variables
and their accurate optimal solutions are all equal zero. The
GA and PSO were implemented using the open source and
well-developed Matlab codes from [31], whereas the KAGA and
KAPSO were implemented by integrating GA and PSO with
DACE (Kriging) [32]. The population size and the maximum
number of iterations for these test algorithms were set to 20 and
50,000, respectively. In order to balance exploitation and ex-
ploration, the crossover probability of each selected parents and
the mutation probability of each offspring for GA and KAGA
were 0.7 and 0.3, respectively, while for KAPSO constriction
coefﬁcients were used. Moreover, mutation is performed by
randomly selectingceil(0.01∗nVar ) variables in the offspring
and generating new values based on Gaussian distribution [24],
[25], where ceil is the ceiling operator and nVar is the total
number of variables. Finally, the ELS was employed in the
standard PSO to avoid the premature convergence.
The results in terms of the mean Optimal Solution (OS),
average number of Function Evaluations (FEs) required to ﬁnd
the OS within the speciﬁed tolerance of 0.01, and the total
Success Rate (SR) of ﬁnding an acceptable optimal solution
for 50 trials obtained from GA, PSO, KAGA and KAPSO are
provided in Table I, where ‘INF’ means that the algorithm
failed to converge to the optimum within the speciﬁed toler-
ance after reaching the maximum number of allowed iterations.
Comparing unassisted GA and PSO with the versions utilizing
Kriging reveals that using this type of surrogate modeling always
improves the performance, in terms of Success Rate, ﬁnding a
better optimum and using smaller number of necessary function
evaluations, sometimes signiﬁcantly. Note that the Kriging as-
sisted approaches were actually consuming more computational
time than the GA and PSO in these tests, because the test
functions are computationally very cheap, while the Kriging
assisted strategies were introduced mainly for solving problems
which have expensive objective function evaluations (e.g., Finite
Element Model). However, it has to be emphasized that the more
complex the objective function evaluation is, the more efﬁcient
the Kriging assisted methods tend to be. Furthermore, the GA
and PSO were visibly trapped in local minima for some test
functions (e.g., Schwefel and Ackley have low success rates),
whereas the assistance of Kriging enabled a global optimum to
be easily found. Kriging may also be helpful in combination with
other optimization algorithms; GA and PSO were chosen here
because of their popularity and availability of relevant codes.
Finally, comparing KAGA with KAPSO suggests that overall
both proposed methods provide similar quality answers; thus it
was decided to use KAGA and KAPSO for the OPF problems
addressed in this paper.

B. IEEE 118 Bus System
This larger-scale system has 4,242 MW active and 1,439 MV ar
reactive power demand with 130 control variables, including 53
active power outputs and 54 terminal voltages of generators, 9
transformers and 14 shunt compensators. The upper and lower
limits for voltage magnitudes of all buses are set to 1.06 pu and
0.94 pu, while the shunt capacitors can compensate a minimum
of 0 to a maximum of 30 MV ar. For solving the OPF problems
the population size and maximum number of iterations for the
proposed algorithms were set to 100 and 10,000, respectively.
For this case, the ‘sigma’ described in (31) was set to 0.01 for
PSO and KAPSO to achieve better optimal results.
In this particular case, we found that the penalty factor used
in IEEE 30 bus system for the load bus voltage and the reactive
power generation constraints were no longer adaptive (i.e., the
penalties for voltage and reactive power, compared with the
objective value, were too small and too large, respectively). As a
result, the voltage magnitudes and the reactive power generated
were easily pushed beyond the speciﬁed limits and trapped at
local optima. Therefore, the penalty values of 5,000 and 0.02
for the load bus voltage and the reactive power generation con-
straints were used instead to deal with the inequality constraint
of state variables. Such settings usually lead the algorithms to
ﬁnd good optimal solutions, but the reactive power generation
may violate the speciﬁed limits because the penalty value is set
too small. In order to address such reactive power generation
violation, the “Reactive Power Enforcement (RPE)” strategy
[33] was employed. The reactive power generation is enforced
to its limit and this “PV” bus is re-deﬁned to “PQ” bus for power
ﬂow calculations, if any violation is detected at the maximum
iteration. This is a very effective strategy to deal with the reactive
